courseTitle: Cloud Deployment, Monitoring, Backup & Job-Ready Capstone

lessons.title: Gathering Real Requirements Before You Deploy Anything

slots.practicalActivity: Write a 5-bullet requirements brief for a real or chosen workload, answering this lesson's five required questions in order: expected traffic/load, compliance requirements, budget constraints, availability needs, and who the users actually are. Then take the vague stakeholder request "we need this live by Friday" and show, in writing, which of those five answers is still missing and what deploying without it would actually risk.
slots.deliverable: A written 5-point requirements brief for your workload, plus your written risk analysis of the "live by Friday" request's missing answers.

lessons.title: Choosing Azure, AWS, or Both for a Given Workload

slots.practicalActivity: Apply this lesson's five real factors (team expertise, specific service capabilities, compliance/data residency, cost, vendor lock-in) to your Lesson 1 workload and write a one-paragraph provider recommendation naming a single provider, or a genuinely justified multi-cloud reason, with at least three of the five factors cited by name.
slots.deliverable: A written provider decision for your workload citing at least three of the lesson's five factors by name, with your specific reasoning.

lessons.title: Sizing Compute and Storage Realistically

slots.practicalActivity: Using your Lesson 1 expected-load number, pick a baseline VM/instance size and justify it in writing from that number — not a guess and not the largest size "to be safe." Then name the exact monitoring data (CPU, memory, storage I/O, request counts) you would check after deployment to right-size it, per this lesson's four-step loop, and state one concrete sign each of over-provisioning and under-provisioning would show in that data.
slots.deliverable: A written baseline size choice justified from your load number, plus the specific monitoring signals that would reveal over- or under-provisioning after deployment.

lessons.title: Designing the Architecture Diagram Before You Build

slots.practicalActivity: Draw an architecture diagram for your Lesson 1-3 workload showing all three required elements — network layout, compute tiers, and data flow — by tracing one full request from the user through every tier to storage and back. Deliberately check whether any tier in your sketch ends up needing direct access to a tier it shouldn't, the exact kind of problem this lesson says is cheap to catch on paper and expensive to catch after deployment.
slots.deliverable: A hand-drawn or diagrammed architecture sketch for your workload with network layout, compute tiers, and a traced data-flow path, plus a written note on any tier-access problem it caught.

lessons.title: The Real Deployment Order: Network First

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the real ordered command sequence this lesson teaches — resource group, then VNet/VPC, then subnets, then NSGs/security groups, then compute — using real az/aws syntax. Then deliberately run (or write) `az vm create` or `aws ec2 run-instances` against a resource group with no network yet, omitting the subnet flag, and capture the actual error text it returns.
slots.deliverable: Your written five-step ordered deployment sequence with real command syntax, plus the captured error text from attempting to deploy compute before the network exists.

lessons.title: Deploying VNets, VPCs, and Subnets

slots.practicalActivity: Using this lesson's exact `az network vnet create` / `aws ec2 create-vpc` and subnet-create commands, create (or fully write out) a /16 VNet/VPC with three /24 subnets for a web, app, and data tier, deliberately leaving the remaining address space unused for future tiers. Run `az network vnet subnet list` or `aws ec2 describe-subnets` to confirm the three CIDR ranges came out correct.
slots.deliverable: Executed or fully written commands creating a /16 VNet/VPC with three correctly sized /24 subnets, plus the subnet-list verification output.

lessons.title: Deploying NSGs and Security Groups Correctly the First Time

slots.practicalActivity: For the three subnets from Lesson 6, write the real `az network nsg rule create` / `aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress` commands implementing one least-privilege rule set per tier: nsg-web allows 443 only from a known range, nsg-app allows the app port only from snet-web, nsg-data allows the DB port only from snet-app. Confirm none of your three rule sets uses `*` or `0.0.0.0/0` anywhere.
slots.deliverable: Three written or executed NSG/security-group rule sets, one per tier, each scoped to a specific source and port with no wildcard rule anywhere.

lessons.title: Verifying Network Connectivity Before Moving On

slots.practicalActivity: Deploy (or script) one disposable test VM/instance per tier using the Lesson 7 rules, then run both positive and negative checks this lesson requires: confirm vm-test-web reaches the internet on 443 while vm-test-data cannot be reached from the internet at all, and vm-test-app can reach vm-test-data on the DB port while itself staying unreachable from the internet. Use `nc`/`curl`/`Test-NetConnection`, or Azure Network Watcher / AWS Reachability Analyzer.
slots.deliverable: A written verification log listing both the allowed and the blocked connection attempts for every tier boundary, each with a pass/fail result.

lessons.title: Deploying VMs and EC2 Instances into the Network

slots.practicalActivity: Launch (or fully write) the real `az vm create` / `aws ec2 run-instances` command explicitly naming the Chapter 2 VNet/subnet/NSG (or VPC/subnet/security group), including the `--public-ip-address ""` override for a private app-tier instance. In a separate scratch test, omit the subnet flag entirely and write down exactly what default network Azure or AWS silently substitutes instead of failing the launch.
slots.deliverable: The executed or fully written launch command naming the real subnet/NSG, plus written confirmation of the specific default network the platform substitutes when that flag is omitted.

lessons.title: Deploying Storage Accounts and S3 Buckets

slots.practicalActivity: Create a storage account with `--allow-blob-public-access false --default-action Deny` plus a network rule scoped to your app subnet, or an S3 bucket with all four `put-public-access-block` settings set to `true`. Then attempt a request to the storage from outside the allowed network or identity and confirm it is actually denied, not just configured to look denied.
slots.deliverable: The storage account/bucket creation and lock-down commands, plus a captured failed access attempt proving deny-by-default is actually enforced.

lessons.title: Wiring Compute to Storage Correctly

slots.practicalActivity: Assign the Lesson 9 VM a system-assigned managed identity (or the Lesson 9 EC2 instance an instance profile) and grant it a role/policy scoped to only the one storage account/bucket from Lesson 10 — for example `Storage Blob Data Contributor`. Confirm in writing that the VM/instance could not reach storage before this grant and can immediately after, with no connection string or access key appearing anywhere in the process.
slots.deliverable: Written or captured proof of access denied before the role/policy grant and access allowed immediately after, with zero stored credentials anywhere in the chain.

lessons.title: A Smoke Test: Confirming the Environment Actually Works

slots.practicalActivity: From the VM/instance, authenticated via its managed identity or instance profile, write a test file to the Chapter 3 storage and read it back (`az storage blob upload`/`download` or `aws s3 cp` both directions), then run `curl -I http://localhost/health`. For each of the two checks, write down what a failure there would specifically tell you to investigate first.
slots.deliverable: Captured output of a successful storage round trip and a successful health check, plus written notes on what a failure at each step would point to.

lessons.title: Standing Up Monitoring Before You Need It

slots.practicalActivity: Create the Log Analytics workspace or CloudWatch log group this chapter's alerts will attach to, using `az monitor log-analytics workspace create` or `aws logs create-log-group`. Then write a list distinguishing what your Chapter 3 resources are already reporting automatically (platform metrics) from what still has no log destination, visibility, or alerting configured yet.
slots.deliverable: A created log destination (or fully written creation command), plus a written list separating what's already collected automatically from what monitoring still needs to add.

lessons.title: Configuring the Alerts That Actually Matter

slots.practicalActivity: Configure (or fully write) this lesson's four worked-example alerts — sustained CPU above 85% for 15 minutes, disk free below 15%, a failed health check, and repeated failed logins — each wired to a real Action Group or SNS topic. For each alert, write the one sentence describing what a real person would actually do about it if it fired.
slots.deliverable: Four configured or fully written alert rules, each wired to a notification destination, with one real response action stated per alert.

lessons.title: Avoiding Alert Fatigue from Day One

slots.practicalActivity: Reason through what would happen if your Lesson 14 CPU alert were set to 70% instead of 85% against a web server's normal daytime load — estimate how many times it would likely fire in the first week for completely normal traffic. Then write the specific evidence (for example, "85% never fired across two weeks of real traffic") that would actually justify adding a fifth alert later, rather than guessing one in on day one.
slots.deliverable: A written comparison of the likely false-positive rate at 70% vs. 85%, plus your stated evidence bar for deliberately adding a fifth alert later.

lessons.title: A Monitoring Checklist for a New Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Run this lesson's five-point checklist against your Chapters 1-3 build: metrics configured and confirmed actually flowing, the four alerts configured, each alert actually test-fired (not just assumed to work), the Action Group/SNS topic has a real subscriber, and one dashboard shows CPU/disk/health in a single view. Mark each point pass/fail with real evidence, not assumption.
slots.deliverable: A completed five-point monitoring checklist with pass/fail evidence for every item, including proof at least one alert was deliberately test-fired.

lessons.title: RTO and RPO: What They Actually Mean for a Deployment

slots.practicalActivity: For your own chosen workload, state a real RTO and RPO in plain business terms (for example, "down for 4 hours is tolerable," "losing 1 hour of data is tolerable"). Then show, with the lesson's own reasoning, why a once-daily backup schedule structurally cannot satisfy your stated RPO, and state the minimum backup frequency that RPO actually requires.
slots.deliverable: A written RTO and RPO statement for your workload, plus the specific minimum backup frequency your stated RPO mathematically requires.

lessons.title: Configuring a Real Backup Policy

slots.practicalActivity: Configure (or fully write) an Azure Backup policy or AWS Backup plan with tiered retention — daily points kept a week, weekly kept a month, monthly kept a year — that actually satisfies the RPO from Lesson 17. Tag your resources `Environment=Production` vs. dev/test, and attach a separate, deliberately lighter policy to a dev/test resource that doesn't need the same protection.
slots.deliverable: A configured or fully written tiered-retention backup policy meeting your stated RPO, plus a second, lighter policy for a non-production resource.

lessons.title: Testing a Restore, Not Just Taking Backups

slots.practicalActivity: Actually restore (or fully document the exact steps to restore) one real backup from Lesson 18 into a test or scratch resource, and verify the resulting data is correct and current — not just that the restore command reported success. Write down specifically what you would have missed if you had only trusted the backup job's "completed successfully" log line.
slots.deliverable: A captured or fully documented restore test with a verified result, plus a written note naming the specific gap between "job succeeded" and "restore verified."

lessons.title: Basic Disaster Recovery Planning for a Small Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page DR plan for your environment covering exactly the four real pieces this lesson scopes: known RTO/RPO (Lesson 17), a backup policy that meets them (Lesson 18), the date of your last restore test (Lesson 19), and a named recovery procedure with a named owner — explicitly not an enterprise multi-region failover design.
slots.deliverable: A one-page, four-part DR plan naming specific RTO/RPO numbers, the backup policy, the last restore-test date, and a named recovery-procedure owner.

lessons.title: Why a Deployment Isn't Done Until It's Documented

slots.practicalActivity: Run this lesson's "six-month test" honestly against your own build: name three specific questions (for example, "why is this subnet sized this way," "why does this VM have this role," "where do the backup logs land") and check whether a teammate with no access to you could actually answer them from what's written down today.
slots.deliverable: A written six-month-test result naming your three chosen questions with an honest pass/fail for each, based only on what's actually documented right now.

lessons.title: Writing an Architecture Diagram and Runbook Together

slots.practicalActivity: Write one real runbook entry for your environment (for example, "Web Tier Unresponsive") whose steps reference your architecture diagram by name at each point, exactly as this lesson's worked example does. Then have someone unfamiliar with your environment try to follow it using only the diagram and the runbook text, and note where they got stuck.
slots.deliverable: One written runbook entry with diagram-referenced steps, plus written notes from having someone else attempt to follow it cold.

lessons.title: Documenting for the Next Engineer, Not for Yourself

slots.practicalActivity: Take one real configuration decision from your build (a subnet size, a VM size, a backup retention window, or an alert threshold) and write its documentation two ways: a WHAT-only version and a WHAT+WHY version. Run this lesson's new-hire test on both and write which one actually answers the question a stranger would ask.
slots.deliverable: Both versions of the same documented decision (WHAT-only vs. WHAT+WHY), with your written new-hire-test verdict on which one works.

lessons.title: A Real Handoff Checklist

slots.practicalActivity: Run the full six-item handoff checklist against your own environment: diagram current, runbook written, access actually transferred (not just described), monitoring/alerting contacts updated, backup/DR procedure documented, known issues and technical debt named. For any item that fails, write the specific real problem that failing item would cause for whoever inherits this environment.
slots.deliverable: A completed six-item handoff checklist with pass/fail per item and the specific real consequence named for every item that fails.

lessons.title: The Five Places a New Deployment Usually Breaks

slots.practicalActivity: Write out, without looking, this lesson's five places a deployment usually breaks: network/routing, security group/NSG rules, DNS, IAM/RBAC permission gaps, and resource quota/limit hits. Then invent two realistic "it's broken" tickets against your own environment and map each one to exactly one of the five, explaining why it isn't one of the other four.
slots.deliverable: Your written five-place list from memory, plus two mapped tickets each assigned to one specific place with reasoning for ruling out the others.

lessons.title: Diagnosing Connectivity Failures Systematically

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one real resource in your environment and run this lesson's five-question sequence against it top to bottom — is it running, is there a route, is it allowed through the firewall, does it resolve, is it listening — using the actual `az`/`aws` CLI, `nslookup`/`dig`, and `netstat`/`ss` commands. Record the exact command and result for each question, and note which question you would have stopped at if it had failed.
slots.deliverable: A captured or written walkthrough of all five diagnostic questions run against one real resource, with the exact command used for each step.

lessons.title: Diagnosing Permission and Identity Failures

slots.practicalActivity: Take one AuthorizationFailed/403-style error (this lesson's worked `listKeys` example, or a real one from your own build) and run the four-step trace: identify the calling identity, list its current role assignments, compare them against exactly what the denied action requires, then assign the narrowest role at the narrowest scope. Write why that's narrower than the first fix (e.g. subscription-wide Contributor) that would have technically "worked."
slots.deliverable: A written four-step permission trace ending in a specific narrow role/policy assignment, with your reasoning for why it's narrower than the easier, wrong fix.

lessons.title: When to Roll Back vs. When to Fix Forward

slots.practicalActivity: Write two incident scenarios against your own environment: one where the fix is small, fully understood, and low-blast-radius, and one where half the environment is degraded and the fix isn't clear yet. Apply this lesson's factor list to each and write which choice — rollback or fix-forward — you'd make, naming the specific factors that tipped the decision.
slots.deliverable: Two written incident scenarios, each with a rollback-vs-fix-forward decision and the specific factors from the lesson that justified it.

lessons.title: Capstone Part 1: Planning and Network Deployment

slots.practicalActivity: Playing the engineer for Harrow Peak Outfitters, carry out Lesson 29's real plan yourself: apply the five requirements questions to Dana Oyelaran's stated constraints (6 AM-10 PM uptime, US data residency, modest budget, no 24/7 ops team), size the app VM to Standard_D2s_v5 from the stated real usage data, design the three-subnet `harrowpeak-prod-vnet` (10.20.0.0/16: app/data/mgmt), and write the three NSG rules — app-subnet allows only 443 inbound, mgmt-subnet allows RDP/SSH only from the one static office IP, data-subnet allows 1433 only from app-subnet. Verify a test host in app-subnet can reach the data-subnet private endpoint on 1433.
slots.deliverable: Your own written or deployed version of Harrow Peak's VNet/subnet/NSG layer, plus the app-to-data connectivity verification on port 1433.

lessons.title: Capstone Part 2: Compute, Storage, and Monitoring

slots.practicalActivity: Continue the Harrow Peak build from Lesson 30: deploy `harrowpeak-app-vm` into app-subnet, `harrowpeakstorage` with a service endpoint restricted to app-subnet, and `harrowpeak-orders-db` behind a private endpoint in data-subnet, then wire the VM's system-assigned managed identity to `Storage Blob Data Contributor` and an Azure AD database user — zero stored connection strings or keys. Run the three-part smoke test (one real order write, one real invoice upload, a config check confirming zero stored secrets) and configure the four alerts this lesson names, routed to one action group.
slots.deliverable: A completed three-part Harrow Peak smoke test (order write, invoice upload, no stored secrets confirmed) plus the four configured alerts routed to one action group.

lessons.title: Capstone Part 3: Backup, Documentation, and Handoff

slots.practicalActivity: Finish Harrow Peak's build to Dana's stated RTO of 4 hours / RPO of 1 hour: configure continuous transaction-log backups for `harrowpeak-orders-db`, a daily backup for the app VM, and blob soft-delete/versioning/GRS for storage, then actually run all three restore tests (recover a deleted test invoice, point-in-time-restore the database to a scratch copy, boot the VM from a recovery point). Write the as-built architecture diagram, runbook, and handoff checklist, then diagnose this lesson's real 403 blob-upload error with Chapter 7's method — ruling out RBAC, finding the storage account's network-rule firewall misconfiguration (mgmt-subnet allowed instead of app-subnet) — and fix it.
slots.deliverable: Three completed restore tests, a written handoff package (diagram, runbook, checklist), and a documented trace of the 403 error from symptom to the actual storage-firewall fix.

lessons.title: Job-Ready Foundation Review and What's Next

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own "walk me through a deployment you've done" interview answer using the completed Harrow Peak Outfitters project as the real example. Name at least one specific decision from Lessons 29-31 (for example, the data-subnet NSG scoped only to app-subnet's range, or the managed identity replacing a stored credential) that only worked because of something taught in an earlier course in this stage, naming that earlier course by title. State whether Cloud Support Engineer or Junior Cloud Engineer is your first target role and why.
slots.deliverable: A written, interview-ready project walkthrough citing one decision traced back to a specific earlier course by name, plus your stated target role and reasoning.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course — and the entire seven-course Job-Ready Foundation stage it closes — a student can take a real small-business cloud migration from a stakeholder conversation to a fully operating, documented, handed-off environment: gathering real requirements before touching a console, choosing a provider and sizing compute from actual numbers instead of guesses, deploying network, compute, and storage in the correct dependency order with least-privilege NSGs and identity-based access that never stores a credential, standing up a small high-confidence alert set instead of noisy over-alerting, configuring and actually restore-testing backups against a stated RTO and RPO, documenting the result for a stranger rather than for themselves, and diagnosing a real production error (a stale rule, a missing role, a misconfigured firewall) systematically instead of guessing — exactly the Harrow Peak Outfitters project this capstone walks through end to end, from Dana Oyelaran's six-year-old warehouse server to a monitored, backed-up, documented Azure environment with a found-and-fixed 403 error along the way. That is a real, complete, portfolio-ready answer to "walk me through a deployment you've done," and it is what qualifies a graduate of this stage for Cloud Support Engineer and Junior Cloud Engineer roles today, with the path's Advanced Specialization stage — starting with Terraform, Bicep & Infrastructure as Code — as the deliberate next step rather than a guess at what to learn next.
